summary:
Malaysia criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity under federal and state law. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature", covering oral and anal sex, for any person regardless of gender or consent; the maximum penalty is 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping, recorded as mandatory. The offence reaches foreign nationals and tourists, and sodomy was first criminalised in 1871. Section 377D adds "gross indecency", an undefined offence carrying up to two years that remains a discretionary prosecutorial tool.

Every state and the federal territories (Kuala Lumpur, Putrajaya) maintain Sharia enactments criminalising same-sex activity and gender nonconformity, including provisions against "a man posing as a woman". These apply only to Muslims, with penalties of up to three years, a RM5,000 fine and six strokes of the cane. Since the 1980s all 13 states have passed Sharia enactments institutionalising discrimination against trans people; all 13 bar Muslim men from "dressing as women" and three also bar "women posing as men", enforced by state Islamic religious departments with no legal definition of transgender dressing. The Selangor and Kelantan codes and the Sharia Criminal Code (I) Enactment 2019 cover "sodomy" and "sexual intercourse against the order of nature".

The Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Syariah provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, without decriminalising anything under the Penal Code. The High Court separately denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted, but raids on queer venues are documented: a Kuala Lumpur gay bar was raided by police and religious enforcement in August 2018, a Halloween party with LGBTQ participants was raided in 2022, and 11 shopping malls were raided in May 2023 over Swatch Pride watches. In November 2024 Kelantan approved amendments to its entertainment law banning activities that promote LGBTQ behaviour.

On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur and arrested 208 men under section 377B, the largest such raid since 2022, with media pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details leaked; 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground under 377B, yet release was delayed, with over 130 held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid; on 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

State-sanctioned targeting of trans people is documented. In July 2020 Religious Affairs Minister Zulkifli Mohamad Al-Bakri announced he had given the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons; the International Commission of Jurists condemned the order and demanded its revocation. In 2021, 122 religious officers were mobilised to hunt Nur Sajat over "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and gained UNHCR protection. Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events and media content were censored.

Violence against trans women is documented: a transgender woman was killed in Klang, a Kuala Lumpur suburb, in a report of 25 June 2019, the third such killing of a trans woman in Malaysia in fewer than two months, alongside police mistreatment and impunity. The most recent documented killing in this record is from 2019; no later instance is documented. The 2014 record documents the 2011 strip-search and sexual assault of Victoria by religious officials, repeated arrests of one woman over 20 times, and the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Identity documents are a live battleground. In August 2016 the Kuala Lumpur High Court ordered the National Registration Department to update a trans man's identity card with his gender identity and chosen name, reasoning that Article 5(1) of the Federal Constitution guarantees a right to live with dignity as a male, but this judgment was overturned on appeal in 2017. The Registration Department routinely rejects gender-marker changes; the only successful documented change is historical, in 1975. A 1982 National Fatwa Council fatwa holds that sex is determined at birth and remains so after sex reassignment surgery, ending domestic sex-reassignment surgery for Muslims; it was never gazetted and so is not legally binding, but it bars Muslims from the procedure unless intersex. There is no explicit visa rule for transgender visitors; the only entry/deportation policy stated in the sources is a 2001 statement by then-Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad that Malaysia would deport any visiting foreign cabinet minister or diplomat who is gay.

Sharia courts may commit women convicted of musahaqah to an approved home for up to six months (Federal Territories s.56, Kedah s.52, Selangor s.54, Sarawak s.53), and may order cross-dressing or other offenders into counselling or rehabilitation in a religious institution: up to six months in Kelantan (s.19-20) and Pahang (s.66), extended to up to one year by Terengganu's 2022 amendment. Trans people face discriminatory denial of health care and employment alongside arbitrary arrest, physical and sexual assault, and imprisonment; prison terms run from four months to three years with male-ward sexual violence. Conversion therapy is practised and openly promoted by politicians and religious leaders. The National Blood Centre of Malaysia prohibits homosexuals and bisexuals from donating blood.

There are no Malaysian laws protecting the LGBTQ community against discrimination and hate crimes, and no same-sex marriage or anti-discrimination law. Same-sex couples have no route to recognition; at Cambridge Union in June 2019 Mahathir said Malaysia cannot accept same-sex marriage. The 1982 fatwa additionally ruled that marriages involving transgender people are invalid, though not gazetted; the single exception is the 1975 sharia marriage of transgender woman Sari Kartina in Johor Bahru. Hate speech rules do cover orientation: the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Content Code 2022, s.6.1(ii), defines hate speech as material that denigrates or devalues a person on grounds including sexual orientation, enforced via s.211 of the Communications and Multimedia Act. In 1994 the government banned anyone homosexual, bisexual or transsexual from state-controlled media. Adoption is orientation-neutral under the Adoption Act 1952 and Registration of Adoption Act 1952, with no restriction on a single person adopting regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects: Reuters reported in August 2023 that LGBT people in Malaysia face growing fears as Islamist opposition blocks reform efforts, and LGBTQ rights are not pursued by any political party. In July 2023 the band The 1975 was forced to cut short its Good Vibes Festival set after Matty Healy criticised the country's anti-LGBTQ laws and kissed a bandmate, an instance of artist pressure intersecting with the legal climate.

Human Rights Watch's 10 August 2022 report "I Don't Want to Change Myself" drew on interviews with 73 LGBT people in Malaysia conducted between 2018 and 2021 across seven states, plus journalists and lawyers. The Human Dignity Trust country profile places Malaysia among jurisdictions that criminalise same-sex conduct and lists active litigation alongside cases from Mauritius and Namibia. The United Nations Development Programme and the Asia Pacific Transgender Network have published a joint publication on Malaysia.
